title: The New World of Work Is Already Here. Are You Ready for It?
excerpt: AI, automation and remote work are quietly rewriting what employers hire for, in Lagos as much as in London. Here is what the WEF and ILO data actually say, and the practical moves to make this year.
content:
Walk into a banking hall on Broad Street in Lagos around 2012 and you would have met the queue: forty people deep, snaking past the security desk, everyone clutching a paper slip or a chequebook. Behind the glass sat a long row of tellers, and being one of them was a good job. Steady salary, air conditioning, a clear path into branch operations. Walk into that same hall today and the queue has thinned to almost nothing. The customers moved into USSD codes and banking apps, and the counters went quiet. Nobody announced the change. It arrived one transfer at a time, and it landed hardest on the people who assumed the job would always be there.

Here is the uncomfortable part: bank teller is now one of the fastest declining occupations on earth, according to the World Economic Forum's Future of Jobs Report 2025, which gathered the hiring plans of more than 1,000 large employers responsible for over 14 million workers across 55 economies. And here is the hopeful part: the same report expects far more jobs to be created than destroyed. The new world of work is not a story about work ending. It is a story about work moving. Your assignment this year is to make sure you are standing where it is moving to, not where it is moving from.

What the numbers actually say

The headline figures deserve a slow read. Between 2025 and 2030, employers expect 170 million new jobs to be created worldwide and 92 million to be displaced, a net gain of 78 million. Put differently, about 22 percent of today's formal jobs will churn in just five years. Some 86 percent of employers expect AI and information processing technologies to transform their business by 2030. And on average, employers estimate that 39 percent of the skills workers use today will be transformed or outdated within that same window.

Read that last number again. Roughly two fifths of your current skill set has an expiry date, and the date is close. That is not a reason to panic. It is a reason to plan. This change will not punish people for having the wrong job title today. It will punish the ones who stop learning.

Fading roles, rising roles

The report names names, and the pattern is hard to miss once you see it. Roles built on routine, rule-based tasks are shrinking, while roles that combine technology with judgment are growing fastest in percentage terms.

Declining fastest (part of 92 million jobs expected to be displaced by 2030)Growing fastest (part of 170 million new jobs expected by 2030)
Postal service clerksBig data specialists
Bank tellers and related clerksAI and machine learning specialists
Data entry clerksFintech engineers
Cashiers and ticket clerksSoftware and application developers
Administrative assistants and executive secretariesRenewable energy and environmental engineers

One caution before you conclude that everyone must become an AI engineer. In absolute numbers, the biggest growth is projected in frontline work: farmworkers, delivery drivers, construction workers, salespersons, nursing professionals and teachers. The future of work is not only laptops. But even those roles are being rewritten around digital tools, which is why the report finds technological literacy among the fastest growing skills across nearly every industry.

The African twist: the problem is job quality, not just jobs

Now bring this home. The modeled estimates published by the World Bank put youth unemployment in sub-Saharan Africa at about 10 percent in 2024, far lower than the crisis figures people trade at parties. The real story sits underneath that number. The ILO's Global Employment Trends for Youth brief for sub-Saharan Africa found that 21.9 percent of young people in the region, about 53 million, were not in employment, education or training in 2023. Among young adults aged 25 to 29 who do work, nearly three in four were in insecure forms of work. And three in five of those locked out entirely were young women.

So the challenge for a graduate in Kano or Kisumu is rarely that there is no work. It is that there is not enough good work nearby. That is exactly why the remote shift matters so much for us. The World Economic Forum's research on global digital jobs counted 73 million jobs in 2024 that can be done fully remotely from anywhere, and projects that figure to reach around 92 million by 2030. Those jobs used to live in London, Toronto and Berlin. Today a product designer in Accra or a data analyst in Nairobi can compete for them without a visa, a relocation budget or anyone's permission. We have written a full playbook on earning globally while living locally if that path calls to you.

What employers are actually hiring for now

Here is the quiet revolution inside all this data: employers are running out of the skills they need, and they know it. In the WEF survey, 63 percent of employers named skill gaps as the biggest barrier to transforming their business, 85 percent plan to prioritise upskilling their workforce, and 70 percent expect to hire people who bring new skills in the door. The most sought after core skill is not coding. It is analytical thinking, which seven out of ten companies consider essential, followed by resilience, flexibility and agility.

Notice what that means for you. When companies hire for skills they cannot find, the person with visible, demonstrable ability starts to beat the person with the older, shinier certificate. A GitHub repository, a portfolio of client work, a dashboard you built for a local business in Johannesburg: these are becoming the strongest currencies in the hiring market. Credentials still matter, but proof is pulling ahead.

Moves to make this year

  • Audit your own role honestly. Write down your ten most common weekly tasks. If most are routine and rule-based, the table above is talking about you, and it is better to hear it now than in a retrenchment letter.
  • Pick one growing skill lane and commit five hours a week. Data, AI literacy, cybersecurity, renewable energy, digital marketing. One lane, one year. Our guide to the digital skills that actually pay in 2026 will help you choose.
  • Build public proof of work. Do three small real projects, even free ones for a church, a shop or an NGO, and put them where an employer can see them.
  • Get remote ready. Reliable power and data plan, professional email, a habit of clear written communication, and a profile on at least one global platform.
  • Strengthen the skills machines are bad at. Persuading, explaining, coordinating people. Analytical thinking tops the employer wish list for a reason.
  • Rewrite your CV around skills and results, not job titles. We show you exactly how in The CV That Gets You Interviews.
  • Put it all into a plan that can bend. A rigid five year plan breaks in a market that churns 22 percent in five years. Build a career plan that survives change instead.

The tellers on Broad Street never got a memo telling them the future had arrived. You just got yours. The data says the next five years will create far more opportunity than they destroy, and for once, geography matters less than it ever has for a young African with skills and a connection. The new world of work is already here. Start this month, not someday, and it will be yours.
